reading.body:
All six tools in this category run models on infrastructure the deployer controls rather than a vendor's, which is why every note attached to them is about supply chain and provenance rather than data handling.

Two are frameworks for training and serving, PyTorch from Meta and the Linux Foundation, TensorFlow and Keras from Google, two are runtimes built for local or edge inference, Ollama and llama.cpp, one is a high-throughput inference engine out of UC Berkeley, vLLM, and one is the hub most of these tools pull models from, Hugging Face Transformers. Ollama and vLLM are flagged for no external data sharing, and llama.cpp, PyTorch, and Hugging Face are flagged for provenance or checkpoint governance, meaning the risk this category tracks is not what a vendor does with your prompts but what a downloaded model file actually contains and whether its lineage can be verified.

This is a compute story as much as a governance one. Self-hosting a model still requires buying or renting the hardware to run it, so this category represents the point where AI adoption becomes a hardware and power decision rather than a subscription decision. The data here does not say how large these deployments typically are, what hardware they run on, or how widely each tool is actually used, only what each one is built to do and what it is watched for.
